one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban uses Manalese v. Ferreras (Nov 25, 2024, per J. Alfredo Benjamin S. Caguioa, Third Division 5-0) to reiterate the hornbook doctrine that buyers must examine very well the property, item, or goods being sold; the relevant deeds of sale; and the original record of the titles. He cautions buyers of lots and condominiums not to be satisfied with verbal or written assurances of sellers and agents -- they should insist on examining the face of, and the entries in, the owner's Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT), and more importantly scrutinize by themselves or through trusted lawyers/agents the Original Certificate of Title (OCT) at the Office of the Register of Deeds of the province or city where the real property is located. Unusual TCT entries should prompt the buyer to desist; liens may be on the OCT but not on the TCT, or coached in technical terms and printed in hardly-readable fonts. The Manalese facts included two indicia of fraud -- sellers who were already dead long before deed execution, and a great price disparity (P250,000 acquisition vs P3.3M resale). The Court instructed the IBP to investigate the Register of Deeds of Angeles City (Atty. Bayani Maniquis) for possible CPR violations, and lamented that despite RA 6732's criminal penalties on fraud-or-deceit in obtaining reconstituted titles and on knowing public-officer assistance, there is 'apparently a dearth if not absence of prosecution' -- a wake-up call to the DOJ for an honest-to-goodness investigation. He then turns to Kaw v. Nodalo (Nov 27, 2024, per J. Henri Jean Paul B. Inting, Third Division 5-0) and recommends Justice Caguioa's concurring opinion as essential reading: sales (whether personal or real property) are perfected at the moment of (1) a meeting of the minds to transfer ownership of (2) a determinate thing (3) upon a price certain in money or its equivalent; the consensual nature means a stipulation that the buyer must first pay before the seller transfers ownership does not divest the agreement of its contract-of-sale character. Starting in 1960, jurisprudence created the distinct 'contract to sell,' in which title remains with the seller until full payment. As a rule, the seller's delivery (or 'tradition') transfers ownership; a notarized document is equivalent to actual or physical delivery -- though the notarized deed may clearly or inferentially reserve ownership until full payment. Once the three elements are satisfied, buyers may occupy, use, rent out, repair, mortgage, pledge, or otherwise deal with the property as they desire and cannot be evicted even if the full price has not been paid -- the seller's remedy is collection, not ownership reversal. Jurisprudence has ruled that a deed is a 'contract to sell,' not a 'contract of sale,' when (1) a separate deed of absolute sale is needed upon full payment, (2) the seller is granted a unilateral right to cancel, and (3) the buyer shall be a mere lessee until full payment. Finally, the mere denomination of an agreement as a 'contract to sell' will not necessarily determine its true nature -- what would is its provisions, 'in like manner, a beauty title does not necessarily determine the inner character of the lady.'
